sections.title: Scripture, History, and Coercive Power
sections.weightRationale: This section tests whether violent scriptural commands, religious rule, dissent sanctions, and covenant interpretation connect Christianity to coercive harm.

sections.title: Health, Family, and Social Harm
sections.weightRationale: Direct medical harms and family rejection are assessed with broad beneficial-outcomes evidence and the specific cross-country reply about homonegativity.

sections.title: Cross-National Outcomes and Climate Policy
sections.weightRationale: Country-level welfare and climate-policy claims share a dispute about population comparisons, causal controls, and competing empirical evidence.

sections.title: Faith, Science, and Evidence
sections.weightRationale: This section addresses whether faith resists scientific evidence or means warranted trust, including intelligence, evolution, linguistic, and medical-trust replies.

sections.title: Causation, Benefits, and Interpretive Responsibility
sections.weightRationale: These exchanges test the required causal standard, the interpretation of claimed benefits, and responsibility for recurrent harmful uses of Christian teaching.

responseComponents.component: claim that faith impairs rational thought
responseComponents.description: Uses correlation limits, later studies, and cross-cultural reversals to deny that religiosity causes lower analytical intelligence.

responseRepairs.rationale: Jones explicitly introduces the intelligence research as an answer to Aron's claim that Christianity encourages less rational thinking.

responseComponents.description: Uses acceptance rates and creationism history to deny that Christianity entails rejecting evolution.

responseRepairs.rationale: The evolution discussion answers Aron's opening science-rejection claim, not the separate climate-policy claim.

responseComponents.component: definition of faith as evidence-resistant belief
responseComponents.description: Appeals to Greek usage and biblical contexts to recast faith as evidence-responsive commitment.

responseRepairs.rationale: Jones expressly quotes and disputes Aron's definition of faith, so the restored epistemic claim is the actual antecedent.

responseComponents.component: present force of violent Old Testament commands
responseComponents.description: Argues that old-covenant laws are fulfilled and do not govern Christians under the new covenant.

responseRepairs.rationale: The covenant argument specifically answers Aron's cited Old Testament commands, not his broader conflict classification.

responseComponents.component: opposition between faith, trust, and evidence
responseComponents.description: Tests whether faith language can describe warranted trust in evidence-backed medical advice.

responseRepairs.rationale: The medical analogy answers Aron's substantive faith definition, not his concession about lacking Greek specialists.

responseComponents.description: Argues that recurring atrocity-justifying interpretations make the religious system predictably dangerous.

responseRepairs.rationale: Aron's culminating interpretation argument returns to Jones's misuse defense; the adjacent homonegativity study is not its actual target.

inferenceSummary.premise: The cited biblical passages prescribe severe violence against unbelief and religious difference.

inferenceSummary.conclusion: Christian scripture supplies a direct pathway to dangerous conduct.

addedMoves.speaker: Aron Ra
quoteEligibleExactSpans: faith is not just a synonym of trust
addedMoves.claimSummary: Religious faith relies on authority, fallacies, or subjective impressions rather than scientific evidence and therefore impairs evidence-sensitive reasoning.
addedMoves.reasonSummary: Aron contrasts faith with trust, lists scientific claims believers may reject, and says Christianity requires belief in unevidenced supernatural claims despite contrary evidence.

inferenceSummary.premise: Faith requires or protects commitments not grounded in scientific evidence.
inferenceSummary.inference: Commitments insulated from contrary evidence weaken the believer's ability to correct false beliefs.
inferenceSummary.conclusion: Christian faith creates an epistemic danger by impairing reason.

additionRationales.repairPurpose: Restores the specific Old Testament violent-command antecedent that the existing covenant reply actually answers.
Restores the omitted opening epistemic claim actually answered by four distinct con arguments and replaces broad or incorrect links.

sectionRationales.scripture-history-and-coercion: Four pro rows are necessary and nonmergeable: conflict attribution, secular-law protection, violent scriptural commands, and dissent punishment use different evidence and mechanisms.
sectionRationales.health-family-and-social-harm: Medical misinformation, treatment denial, and family rejection are distinct harms; broad benefits and the homonegativity study answer different generalization levels.
sectionRationales.cross-national-outcomes-and-climate: Country welfare and climate policy are distinct, while multivariate analysis, climate data, and study-weight arguments are nonduplicative replies.
sectionRationales.faith-science-and-evidence: Four con rows are necessary and nonmergeable: intelligence, evolution, Greek lexical meaning, and medical trust use different warrants against one thesis.
sectionRationales.causation-benefits-and-interpretation: Attribution, doctrine studies, placebo characterization, unfamiliar-study caution, interpretation, and words-misuse form a coherent causal exchange.

selectionBalanceRationale: The inventory is balanced overall; the faith section has four independent con answers but only two bounded pro claims because those replies test different warrants against one thesis.

intervals.reason: Opening question fragment, applause, and procedural interruption reviewed but not selected.
Historical violence and coercive scripture reviewed; selected both causal classification and the violent-command antecedent needed by the covenant reply.
Coercion, dominionism, discrimination, and institutional examples reviewed; the selected move captures the governing life-and-liberty mechanism.
Medical harms and the opening faith-versus-scientific-evidence claim reviewed; retained direct medical mechanisms and restored the epistemic antecedent.
Social-outcome and climate arguments selected as distinct empirical claims.
Applause, moderator travel remarks, speaker introduction, and setup are procedural and unscored.
Opening thanks and burden framing reviewed; selected the developed attribution-error and necessary-cause argument.
Meta-analytic evidence and transition to intelligence reviewed; selected the aggregated-benefit case.
Intelligence and evolution arguments selected separately because they use distinct evidence and conclusions.
Faith-language, Thomas, Hebrews, and covenant interpretation reviewed and represented by two distinct textual moves.
Replies to national comparisons and climate claims selected; remaining material summarizes the burden and offers sources.
Applause, music, and moderator cross-examination instructions are procedural.
Early cross-examination reviewed; selected the placebo/doctrine challenge and its direct causal-evidence answer, with later faith discussion substantially repeating the same dispute.
Dissent sanctions, Thomas, required belief, fundamentalism, and interpretive misuse reviewed; selected the coercion mechanism and motion-level causal reply.
The Greek-expertise concession and medical-trust exchange are expressly represented; the extended back-and-forth elaborates trust versus evidence and triggers audio checks where needed.
Study design, personal experience, placebo interpretation, and unfamiliar-study dispute are represented by the two opposing moves; later career criticism repeats the evidential-standard conflict.
The youth-homelessness claim and Jones's cross-country, noncausal reply are both selected as new material.
The final interpretive-responsibility exchange and words-misuse analogy are both selected through the end of the approved source.

sourceCoverageReview.rationale: The concession on lacking Greek specialists and the distinct cancer/medical-trust analogy are retained; the subsequent repetitions refine the same trust-versus-evidence dispute.
The methodological comparison of one study with a meta-analysis and Aron's placebo/personal-experience reply are independently selected.
The homelessness mechanism is new and selected alongside the 79-country variability and noncausation reply.
The culminating dispute over responsibility for harmful interpretations is selected on both sides, including the concession about misuse of Aron's own words.
